title: Camp 3 close: your rhythm
hookLine: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, a bani and a visit: now assemble a week
last: SIS GANJ — A SHIELD FOR OTHERS.

lines: IT STARTED WITH SEVA AND SHOES.
cards: Nobody does every practice every day. This camp opened with seva nobody saw, and on its second day put you to work on the shoes by your door.
Since then you've listened to kirtan, eaten sitting in a row on the floor, breathed the Name, learned the daily prayers and walked, in your mind at least, into a gurdwara.
Then a whole year of festivals, from Vaisakhi to yesterday. So today isn't a new practice. It's you, with a pen, building a week.

teach.b: Here's what this camp gave you, in six parts. Seva: nishkam seva, service with no audience; daswandh, a tenth for others; and a warning about haumai, the ego that loves credit.
Kirtan: raag, the mood; rahao, the pause; the sangat singing back. Langar: pangat, the same row on the floor.
Simran: the Name on the breath, the amrit vela before dawn, the mala, bead by bead. The banis: Nitnem, from Japji Sahib to Rehras at dusk and Sohila at night.

And the visit: the open door, matha tekna, the chaur, karah prashad, the hukamnama. Then the Sikh year: Vaisakhi, nagar kirtan, gurpurabs, akhand path, chhabeel, Bandi Chhor, Hola Mohalla, Maghi, shaheed, Sis Ganj.
Sikhs have a word for a daily rule, and you've met it: Nitnem. Nit means daily; nem is a rule, a discipline you keep. In Sikh practice, faith isn't left to a mood that comes and goes.

It's built into the day: early morning, evening, night. And into the week: the gurdwara, the langar, the sangat. The Sikh Rehat Maryada sets Nitnem as a daily discipline, and the gurdwara gives the week its shape.
A rhythm holds you on the days motivation doesn't. It isn't a test.
A small rhythm you keep will carry you further than a big one you drop by Thursday.
For a learner or a partner it might be one bani, one meal shared, one quiet morning. Tomorrow a new camp begins: the text itself. Japji Sahib, line by line, starting with its alphabet.

how: Sikhs keep a daily Nitnem of set prayers at dawn, dusk and night, do simran, and go to the gurdwara weekly for kirtan, langar and seva; the rhythm grows over years rather than all at once.

o: the prayer said only at a Sikh wedding
the daily rule of prayers a Sikh keeps
a yearly vow taken at a gurdwara festival

games.q: match the practice to its word.
p: the same row on the floor

s: a rhythm is a test you pass or fail
it's an invitation: small and kept, sized to your life.
nit, daily, and nem, a rule or discipline.
a rhythm means every practice, every day
nobody does all of them every day; Nitnem is the daily core, and the rest fits around it.

games.q: you're building your week. which kind of rhythm does this camp suggest?
o: every practice, every day, starting tomorrow.
small lines a bad day could still manage.
games.why: a small rhythm you keep carries you further than a big one you drop by Thursday.

practice: Take a pen, or a note on your phone, and write seven short lines, one for each day of the week, each with one small thing from this camp: a bani, five minutes of simran, an unseen seva, one shabad, a meal shared, and a gurdwara day if one is near.
Keep every line small enough that a bad day could still manage it, with Waheguru at the top if you pray. Then read your seven lines back once, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Nitnem. A daily rule, kept morning, evening and night: your own rhythm, sized to your life.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nit, daily, plus nem, a rule. the daily prayers, and the habit of keeping them.

carryVoice: Your line: you can do this. Small and kept, the rhythm is yours now. Camp three, complete.
